Your first greeting: say hello to Mochi

Python is a language for giving a computer instructions. Our first instruction is print(): it displays text or a number in the Output panel below the editor.

To send a greeting, type print with a lowercase p, open a parenthesis, put your English message inside matching quotation marks, then close the parenthesis. Choose any greeting you like; there is no special message to memorize.
After Run, your exact message appears in Output and in Mochi's bubble. The bubble is our game's visualization of output. Try two different greetings and watch the change before continuing.
The text inside the quotes is your message. Parentheses surround what we want to display. The quotation marks themselves are not printed.
Start with print, followed by parentheses containing your message in quotation marks.
Use quotes for text. Try replacing Hello with Welcome, then run again. You can also try print(5) to display a number.
Use this example to understand the pattern. Write your own greeting, then change it and run again.
Give your greeting a name

A variable is a name that refers to a value. Instead of repeating a message, we can give it the name greeting using =. This assigns a value; it does not compare values.

Write a line assigning your English message to greeting, then display it with print(greeting). Do not put quotes around the variable name: that would print the name as text.
Predict the message first. Run will show a greeting tag and its value beside Mochi, plus the value in Output and his bubble. Write both lines yourself.
The first line assigns the value before the second line uses the name. Changing the assigned value changes the displayed greeting.
Start with the name greeting, then =, then your message in quotes.
On the next line, write print(greeting). Writing print("greeting") displays the word greeting, rather than the variable's value.
Read the example and predict its output. Choose a different message and write your own program.
A new name for the farm

Store your farm's name in farm_name, then display it. Pick your own English name, such as Sunny Farm.

Variable names start with a letter or _; digits may follow. Do not use spaces, a hyphen -, or a reserved word such as for. farm_name and Farm_name are different names: Python is case-sensitive.
When you display farm_name, this game puts that same name on the gate sign. This is a game-specific connection: Python variables do not automatically create signs.
The underscore is part of the variable name. The space in "Sunny Farm" is allowed because it is inside a string, rather than in the variable name.
Use the variable name farm_name and choose your own text value.
Use quotes around the farm name when assigning it, but no quotes around the variable name inside print. Match capitalization in both lines.
You can choose a new farm name instead of the example. Names such as 2farm and farm-name are not valid variable names here.
Plan your first planting bed

How many planting spaces will fit in a bed? Area = length × width. In Python, the multiplication symbol is *.

Create length and width as whole numbers from 1 to 5. Calculate area = length * width, then display area. Write numbers without quotes so we can calculate with them.
Output will show the result, and a countable bed plan will appear over the soil. This visualizes the area; print does not make crops grow.
The result is 6: two rows with three spaces each. Try different dimensions and predict the number before running.
First choose a numeric length and width, without quotation marks.
Printing 6 alone is not the task. Calculate it using length and width, then display area.
Change one dimension and predict the new number of spaces. The example shows the method; you can choose different numbers.
A note for the reader

A comment starts with #. The rest of that line is a note for the reader; Python does not execute it. We use English code comments in these activities.

Write a short program that adds two numbers in total and displays it. Add an English comment and run, then remove only the comment and run again. You can also start without the comment.
Compare Output with and without the comment: it stays the same if the instructions are unchanged. A # inside a quoted string is part of the text.
The result is 5, with or without the comment. Removing an assignment or print instruction is different from removing a comment.
Write an addition and print(total). Add a line beginning with # and an English note.
Run once with the comment and once without it, keeping instructions and values unchanged. We need both attempts to compare them.
After the first run, change only the comment. Keep the numbers and variable names, then compare the output.
